newsitem.title: USA: Executive, banker settle insider suit on PNC Bank deal.
newsitem.headline: Executive, banker settle insider suit on PNC Bank deal.

text.p: A furniture executive and a banker agreed to pay $136,209 to settle insider trading charges arising from the 1993 takeover of First Eastern Corp. by PNC Bank Corp, regulators said Thursday.

Harry Morgan, 67, president of BMC Inc., a furniture company in Scranton, Pa., and the banker, John Martines, 49, agreed to the settlement without admitting or denying wrongdoing, the Securities and Exchange Commission said.
The case against a third defendant, John Walsh III, 50, a broker and director with Rutherfod, Brown & Catherwood, is continuing, SEC lawyer Greg Bruch said.

According to a civil complaint filed by the SEC in a federal court in Pennsylvania, Morgan, who was then a director of First Eastern, first tipped a friend about the possible merger deal. The friend, who was not identified in the lawsuit, bought First Eastern shares and made $25,093 in illegal profits.

Morgan also told Martines, president of the L.A. Bank in Lake Ariel, Pa., about the impending deal days before its announcement on July 27, 1993, the complaint said. Martines, who was Morgan's business client, bought First Eastern shares through Rutherford, making a $7,175 profit when the shares were sold after the deal was announced.
Martines also passed on the confidential information to three friends, who bought First Eastern shares, making $16,342. Martines' friends are not charged in the case.

Morgan, who did not trade, was charged for breaching his fiduciary duty to First Eastern shareholders and for tipping off Martines despite his duty to maintain strict confidentiality about the merger negotiations.

Walsh allegedly bought shares of First Eastern in his wife's account after learning of the proposed merger deal from Martines' broker, whom he (Walsh) supervised. Walsh also urged six clients to buy First Eastern shares. The SEC said Walsh and the clients made a profit of $21,228.
Creed Black, a lawyer representing Walsh, said Walsh believes he has done nothing wrong and intended to contest the charges in court. Laywers for Morgan and Martines could not be reached for comment.
